title: Food Tax Cut Approved by Japanese Cabinet
paragraphs: Japan's cabinet has approved a bill to temporarily cut the consumption tax on food, in what would be the first reduction in the tax since it was introduced in 1989.

The bill, approved on October 9, would reduce the consumption tax on food and non-alcoholic beverages from the current 8% to just 1% for two years, starting in April 2027 and ending in March 2029. The standard consumption tax rate of 10%, which has been in place since October 2019, would not change. Dining out and alcoholic drinks would also continue to be taxed at the standard rate.
In addition to the tax cut, the bill would introduce a system of annual cash payments for low- and middle-income earners, with the amount linked to income.

The measure fulfills a promise made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The government hopes the tax cut will ease the burden on households, which have been struggling with rising prices, particularly for food.

The cabinet's approval follows several earlier steps. In August, the cabinet approved the basic policy for the tax cut, and in September, it approved an outline of the tax reform. The government now plans to submit the bill to the current extraordinary session of the Diet, Japan's parliament, and aims to have it passed before the session ends on December 12.

However, the plan has attracted significant criticism. The tax cut and cash benefits together are expected to cost the government about 10 trillion yen, or around $63 billion, over two years. So far, the government has not explained in detail how it will make up for this loss of revenue. Opposition lawmakers have questioned how the funds will be secured, and they have also described the rules on who would receive the cash payments as unclear.

There are also wider concerns about Japan's financial health. The country already has one of the weakest fiscal positions among advanced economies, with a very high level of government debt. Critics worry that the tax cut could make this situation worse.
Even within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, some members have expressed doubts about the plan, and several were absent from a key party meeting in August.
